blocks.title: Why backs get hurt

cold_open.text: Ask any provider with a ruined back which call did it. Most of them cannot tell you. There was no snap, no dropped patient, no incident report — just twenty years of lifts, and then one morning the getting out of bed was different.

evidence_flag.topic: Whether lifting technique training prevents back injury
evidence_flag.textbook_position: Body mechanics training is presented as the primary defense against lifting injury: lift with your legs, keep the load close, do not twist. Learn the technique and apply it, and your back will be protected across a career.
evidence_flag.current_evidence: A Cochrane review of manual material handling advice and assistive devices pooled nine randomized and nine controlled trials — over **21,000 workers** — and found **moderate quality evidence that training, with or without assistive devices, does not prevent back pain or back-pain-related disability** compared with no intervention or an alternative. What has been associated with reduced injury in EMS specifically is engineering the lift out of the job: before-and-after studies of powered stretchers and powered load systems report reductions of roughly 14% in all injuries and 25% in patient-handling injuries.
evidence_flag.uncertainty: Two limits, in opposite directions. The biomechanics of a single lift are not in dispute — a load held at arm’s length really does load the spine far more than one held close — so this is evidence against *training as prevention*, not against technique. And the powered-equipment evidence is observational before-and-after work, not randomized: consistent and large, and a weaker design than the review that found training ineffective.
evidence_flag.source_ref: Verbeek JH et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(6):CD005958 · Pryce R et al., Am J Ind Med 2024

screens.body_md:
**Lifting and moving is the largest source of EMS injury and lost work time.** Chapter 2 said vehicles are what kill you. This is what ends careers instead — slowly, without an incident report, years later.

Most of it is cumulative. Nobody can name the lift that did it, which is exactly what makes it hard to prevent.

There is no single call to review, so there is nothing for a safety process to find.

**The biomechanics are not in dispute.** A load held at arm’s length loads the spine several times more than the same load held close. Twisting under load is a separate mechanism again. Distance and rotation are what hurt you.

So keep it close, keep it short, do not twist, and move your feet instead of turning your back.

**What is in dispute is whether teaching that prevents injury.** It does not appear to. And the thing that does show reductions is removing the lift: powered cots, powered load systems, more hands, a different device.

Back belts have been studied repeatedly and have not shown benefit. Neither has pre-employment strength screening.

**So where is your leverage?** Not in lifting better. In lifting less: the decision made before anyone takes weight about how many people, what device, and what route.

That is block 6.2, and it is the part of this chapter with the strongest claim to keeping you working until you choose to stop.

**One sentence to stop saying.** "Just lift with your legs and you will be fine" is half right and entirely misplaced — advice about one lift, offered as a career-long prevention plan.

It also implies that anyone who gets hurt did it wrong. Twenty thousand workers in eighteen trials suggest otherwise, and they suggest it fairly clearly.

blocks.callback_md:
Not technique — or at least, not technique alone, and that is what the trial evidence says rather than an opinion about it.

What prevents it is the lift you did not do with two people, the device you sent for, the four minutes you waited. **The leverage is in the decision before the lift**, which is why the next block is the most important one in this chapter and takes ten seconds to run.

blocks.title: The decision before the lift

cold_open.text: Third floor, no elevator, a narrow turn on the second landing, and a patient who is heavier than either of you expected. Your partner already has the head end off the ground and is looking at you, waiting. Everything from here is worse than everything before it.

screens.body_md:
**Once weight is off the ground your options have closed.** You cannot send for a device, add a person, or change the route while three people are holding a patient on a staircase.

So the decision happens before anyone touches anything. It takes about ten seconds, and it is free.

Every other block in this chapter is about executing a plan. This one is about having made one.

**Four questions.**

How much does this patient actually weigh — estimated high, not optimistically? What is the route out, including turns, stairs and doorways? Do we have enough people, and how long for more? Which device fits the patient, the space and the condition?

Weight, route, hands, device. Ask them out loud, so your partner hears the answers too.

**The route usually decides it.** A ninety-degree landing can rule out the cot that would have carried the weight for you, at any weight.

Walk it first. The constraint that will decide this call is visible from the bottom of the stairs, and it is invisible from beside the patient.

**Waiting is almost always affordable.** For a stable patient, eight minutes for a second crew costs nothing clinically and buys the difference between a routine move and an injury.

The exceptions are real — deterioration, danger — and they are exceptions. Difficulty is not one of them, and neither is being busy.

**Agree a stop word before you lift**, and agree who calls the count. Anyone can stop it, nobody argues in the moment, and it is discussed afterward.

If you realize mid-lift that the plan is wrong, set down in a controlled way and re-plan. A controlled abort is available at every moment, and almost nobody uses it — because stopping feels like failing, right up until somebody is hurt.

blocks.callback_md:
At the bottom of the stairs, before either of you went up — and it was decided by not being asked.

Weight, route, hands, device. Ten seconds on the sidewalk would have produced a stair chair, a third pair of hands, or a plan for that landing. **Right now the only correct move is the one nobody likes**: call the stop, set him down, and answer the four questions you skipped.

blocks.title: Technique and team communication

cold_open.text: Four people, one patient, and someone says "ready?" Two of you lift on the word ready. One lifts on a count of three that never came. The fourth is still finding a grip, and for about a second the whole load is on one person’s lumbar spine.

screens.body_md:
**A sound lift is four things.** A stable base — feet apart and planted, one slightly ahead. A neutral back, bending at the hips and knees. The load close to the body throughout. Smooth movement, without twisting.

Worth doing on every lift. Not, by itself, enough to keep you uninjured across a career, which is what 6.1 was about.

**Name who calls the count, and agree the words.** "Ready, set, lift" and "lifting on three" give different answers to when the weight moves, and half a crew will guess.

One voice, agreed in advance, saying the same words every time. That is the whole of it, and it is what was missing above.

**Everyone confirms ready before the count.** A verbal yes from each person, not an assumption from the fact that nobody objected.

The fourth person still finding a grip is the one who did not get asked. It costs one second and it is where team lifts fail. Ask by name if you have to.

**Say the specific thing, immediately.** "Losing it — setting down on three" tells three other people exactly what happens next. "Hurry up" tells them to go faster into a failure.

Same rule as chapter 4: name the problem, before it happens, not after. A failing grip is the clearest case there is, because everyone else can act on it instantly.

**Set down on a second count.** Concentration drops the moment the weight is up, and a large share of drops and strains happen on the way down.

Move your feet to turn rather than twisting. And if you need to change your grip, set the load down first — regripping under load is when things get dropped, and the patient is what gets dropped.

blocks.callback_md:
A named voice and agreed words.

Nobody was careless. Four people heard an ambiguous cue and resolved it four different ways, which is exactly what an ambiguous cue is for. **One person calls it, everyone confirms ready first, and the words are the same every time** — and there is a second count for setting down, because the way down is where this usually goes wrong.

blocks.title: Carrying, reaching, pushing, pulling

cold_open.text: You never lifted anything heavy today. You reached across a bed to log roll someone, held a door with one arm for four minutes, pulled a cot up a curb, and leaned over a car seat. Your back hurts anyway, and there is nothing to write an incident report about.

screens.body_md:
**Push rather than pull wherever you can.** Pushing lets you put body weight behind the load and keeps it in front of you where you can see it. Pulling loads the back and hides the load behind you.

And push between waist and shoulder height. Lower bends you forward; higher removes your leverage.

Where you must pull, keep it low and close and walk backward rather than leaning.

**Reaching is the quiet one.** Keep the back neutral, avoid hyperextension, and do not reach more than about fifteen to twenty inches in front of you with any weight.

The fix for a long reach is almost always your feet. Move closer rather than extending further — and that is the whole of the log roll problem.

**A log roll combines three mechanisms at once**: a long reach, a sustained hold, and usually a twist, at bed height.

Get the bed to a workable height if you can, put people on both sides, and do not solve the distance by reaching further. It is one of the most repeated postures in the job.

**Time under load is its own exposure.** Muscles fatigue under a static hold and the burden shifts progressively onto passive structures.

So holding a door, a limb or a cot rail "just for a minute" during a long extrication is worth handing over rather than enduring. The weight never changed; what it is resting on did.

**A wheeled device stops being one on the wrong surface.** Gravel, grass, snow, a curb.

Recognize that before you are halfway across it, and change the plan — four people carrying, or a device suited to the ground. Forcing a cot across deep gravel with two people is how cots tip and backs go. The surface changed the task, so change the plan with it.

blocks.callback_md:
All of them, a little, which is the point.

The reach across the bed, the four-minute static hold, the pull above shoulder height, the lean into a car seat. None produced a moment worth reporting and each loaded the spine in a way a textbook lift would not have.

**Cumulative loading is what ends careers**, and it never arrives as an incident. It arrives as a morning.

blocks.title: Emergency, urgent and non-urgent moves

cold_open.text: Two calls. In the first, a patient is on a soft bed in cardiac arrest. In the second, a patient with a hip injury is at the end of a long carry and everyone is tired. Both crews are about to move a patient in a way that would not survive review.

screens.body_md:
**Three categories, sorted by why you are moving.**

**Emergency** — immediate danger to patient or crew. **Urgent** — the patient’s condition requires moving them in order to assess or treat. **Non-urgent** — everything else, which is most of your calls.

The equipment follows from the category, not the other way round.

Most of the errors here are non-urgent moves being run as though they were urgent ones.

**An emergency move accepts the risk of aggravating an injury** because the alternative is worse: fire, a hazardous atmosphere, an unstable vehicle.

Or a clinical necessity with no external danger at all — a patient in arrest on a soft bed, where compressions dissipate into the mattress. The surface is the emergency.

**If you are dragging someone, pull along the long axis of the body** and support the head as far as you can. Clothes drag, blanket drag, shoulder drag.

Never sideways, never by one limb, never by the ankles. You are accepting risk to the spine, not ignoring it, and the direction of pull is how you keep that honest.

**Rapid extrication has four indications**: the scene is unsafe, the patient’s condition cannot be managed in the vehicle, the patient blocks access to someone more critical, or they are deteriorating and cannot wait.

A patient who simply wants out of the car is not one of them, however reasonable the request sounds at the time.

**Difficulty is not danger.** A long carry, a short crew or a tired crew are resource problems with resource answers, and none of them justifies an emergency move.

Every emergency move trades one risk for another. Write down which risk you were buying down — "rapid extrication due to fuel leak" is a defensible sentence, and "moved quickly" is not.

blocks.callback_md:
The first. A patient in arrest on a soft bed needs the floor before anything else you do will work, and that is an emergency move for a clinical reason with no danger anywhere on the scene.

The second is a tired crew at the end of a long carry, which is a resource problem wearing an emergency’s clothes. **Difficulty is not danger**, and the hip is going to be a great deal more difficult tomorrow.

blocks.title: Equipment and positioning

cold_open.text: A patient in severe respiratory distress, sitting bolt upright and gripping the edge of the bed, and a cot that is flat. Your partner starts lowering the back rest so they can be strapped in properly for transport.

screens.body_md:
**The space, the injury and the distance pick the device.** Stair chair for a conscious patient and a narrow staircase. Scoop where a patient must be lifted with minimal movement. Vacuum mattress for a long transport with a spinal indication. Cot for everything else.

Poor choices usually come from picking the device first and then fitting the call to it.

Decide at the bottom of the stairs, where you can still change your mind about all three.

**A scoop earns its place by how it gets under the patient**: it splits, slides in from both sides and closes, with far less movement than a log roll onto a board.

A vacuum mattress earns its place over time — it conforms and spreads pressure, where a rigid board concentrates it and causes pain and tissue injury.

**Position is treatment.** A conscious patient in respiratory distress sits up. An unresponsive patient breathing adequately, with no spinal concern, goes lateral. A vomiting patient who cannot protect their airway goes lateral.

Laying a breathless patient flat because the cot is flat is one of the more common avoidable harms in this chapter.

**The shock position did not survive testing.** Elevating the legs has not shown a clinically meaningful benefit.

Supine, warm, and moving. The transport is the intervention, and the position is one more practice that persisted on plausibility rather than on measurement. Chapter 1 named that pattern; here it is again.

**Before a loaded cot moves**: all straps including chest and legs, rails up, equipment secured, height controlled, both crew in position, and the route checked for the threshold you have not seen.

Cot tip-overs with a patient aboard keep happening, and every one of them is preventable at this list. Run it out loud, the same way every time.

blocks.callback_md:
No. Stop him.

That patient has found the position that lets them breathe, and they found it before you arrived. Forcing them flat for the convenience of the straps can be actively harmful, and there is no rule that requires a supine patient to be secured.

**Position is treatment** — the patient is already administering it, and the job here is to transport it rather than undo it.

blocks.title: Spinal motion restriction

cold_open.text: A stabbing to the neck. He is alert, talking in full sentences, has no weakness anywhere, and he is bleeding steadily. Somebody on scene hands you a cervical collar, because it is an injury to the neck and that is what the collar is for. The trauma center is eleven minutes away.

evidence_flag.topic: Spinal immobilization and the long backboard
evidence_flag.textbook_position: Backboard-centric: apply a cervical collar and secure the patient to a long backboard for any suspected spinal injury, with mechanism of injury as an indication in its own right, and including penetrating trauma.
evidence_flag.current_evidence: Joint guidance from ACS-COT, ACEP and NAEMSP is that the goal is **restriction of motion** — head, neck and torso kept in alignment — achievable with a backboard, scoop, vacuum mattress or the ambulance cot, and driven by **findings rather than mechanism**. It states plainly that there is **no role for spinal motion restriction in penetrating trauma**, where it delays transport and has been associated with worse outcomes. The long board is an extrication tool, not a transport surface.
evidence_flag.uncertainty: Go further than the guidance. A NAEMSP literature review characterizes both spinal motion restriction and spinal immobilization as long-established standards that carry potential for significant patient harm and are **without definitive evidence of clinical benefit**. So two things are true at once: it is indicated in defined circumstances by current guidance, and the evidence that it helps anyone is thin. Being able to say both out loud is part of what this block teaches.
evidence_flag.source_ref: Fischer PE et al., Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61 · NAEMSP literature review

screens.body_md:
**The goal is alignment, not immobility.** Head, neck and torso kept in line — which a vacuum mattress, a scoop, or the cot with the patient properly secured can all achieve.

The change in language is the change in practice. "Restriction of motion by any adequate means" replaced "immobilization on a specific device".

That frees you to use what fits the patient and the space rather than what is on the truck.

**Findings, not mechanism.** Midline spinal pain or tenderness. Any neurological complaint or finding. Altered mental status, including intoxication. A distracting injury, or visible deformity of the spine.

Being in a collision is no longer an indication by itself. That single change is most of the difference from the older practice.

**No role in penetrating trauma.** None. It delays transport for patients whose problem is bleeding, and it has been associated with worse outcomes.

This is the most consequential line in the block, and the one most likely to be contradicted by someone on scene who learned it the other way. Say the reason with it.

**The board is an extrication tool.** A patient extricated on one, with no indications, comes off it for transport in line with your protocol.

Rigid boards cause documented harm over time — pain, pressure injury, restricted breathing. Being carried out on one is not a reason to be transported on one, and the two decisions are made separately.

**And a patient fighting the device is a problem, not a failure of compliance.** Struggling against straps can produce more spinal movement than the restriction prevents.

Ask why they are agitated — hypoxia and head injury are on that list — and weigh honestly whether forcing the device is achieving anything at all.

blocks.callback_md:
No. There is no role for spinal motion restriction in penetrating trauma, and the collar would cover the neck you most need to be watching.

He is bleeding, he is alert, and the trauma center is eleven minutes away. **The collar buys nothing and costs time and visibility.**

If somebody on scene insists, this is worth saying out loud with the reason attached — it is joint guidance from three national bodies, not a local preference.

blocks.title: Bariatric, pediatric and geriatric handling
blocks.learner_title: When the plan does not fit

cold_open.text: Three patients your standard plan was not written for: one heavier than the cot is rated to carry, one too small for the straps to hold, and one whose spine will not straighten onto a flat surface. All three are about to be moved as though none of that were true.

screens.body_md:
**Bariatric: the rated capacity is a limit, not a suggestion.** Check every device in the chain, request extra hands early rather than once you are committed, and assess the route for width, turns and floor strength.

And do not discuss the patient as a problem in front of them. They can hear you, and they have heard it before — often enough that it affects whether they call at all.

**Pediatric: adult cot straps do not restrain a small body.** A size-appropriate restraint device is needed, every time, on every transport length.

A parent holding a child cannot hold them in a collision. Seat the parent where the child can see and touch them — that solves the distress without solving it by removing the restraint.

**Geriatric: the tissue does not tolerate what the equipment assumes.** Thin skin tears from grip and shear. Osteoporotic bone fractures at forces that would not mark a younger patient.

Use a slide sheet or a scoop rather than dragging on skin, and grip broad areas rather than pinching a limb.

**Pad to the patient.** A marked kyphosis will not flatten onto a cot, and forcing it risks fracture as well as being painful and pointless.

Support the position they actually have, with padding under the head and shoulders. The cot is a flat surface; the patient is not obliged to become one, and forcing the point achieves nothing clinical.

**What all three share is that the standard plan assumes a patient none of them is.** The equipment, the straps and the flat surface were designed for somebody else.

Which puts every one of them back in 6.2: the resource and equipment decision, made before anyone lifts, with the four questions asked out loud.

blocks.callback_md:
The plan, before anyone touches anyone.

Check the rating and get more hands for the first. Fit a proper restraint for the second, and put the parent where the child can see them. Pad to the curve for the third, rather than flattening it.

**None of that is discovered mid-move**, and all of it is answered by the same four questions from 6.2 — which is why that block is the one to have automatic.

blocks.title: Integration — a man in a ditch

cold_open.text: A difficult extrication asks every question in this chapter within about ninety seconds, in the dark, with a patient who has an opinion about all of them. Move category, spinal indications, resource decision, device, and how four people carry someone up a soft bank.
cold_open.decision_point: Which of those is the one that protects you?

screens.body_md:
**Five questions, in order, and the order matters.**

Is this an emergency move? Does he meet spinal indications? Do we have the people and the equipment? Which device? And how does the team keep the carry together?

What follows is one call. Four of the five are about the patient, and one of them is about you.

blocks.callback_md:
The resource decision — waiting fourteen minutes for a second unit.

Everything else on that call was about him: the move category, the spinal indication, the choice of a scoop over a board, the count on the bank. All correct, and none of it changes what your spine carried.

**The only decision that reduced the load was the one to not lift 280 pounds out of a ditch with two people**, and he was stable the entire time it took to make it.
