options.text: It is not a decision — you lift what is in front of you
options.rationale: It is the single decision in this chapter with the most leverage.

items.explanation_md: Stand still for ten seconds and answer four questions. That pause is the intervention, and it is free.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select the questions to answer before committing to a move.

options.text: How much does this patient weigh, honestly?
options.rationale: Estimate high rather than optimistically.

options.text: What is the route out, including turns, stairs and door widths?
options.rationale: The route decides the device.

options.text: Do we have enough people, and if not, how long for more?
options.rationale: Waiting four minutes beats a career-ending lift.

options.text: Which device fits the patient, the space and the condition?
options.rationale: Three constraints, and the space is usually the binding one.

options.text: How quickly can we clear this call?
options.rationale: Not a factor in how the patient gets moved.

items.explanation_md: Weight, route, hands, device. Four questions, ten seconds, and they are the part of this chapter with the strongest claim to preventing injury.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: The patient is heavier than your crew can safely manage and help is eight minutes away. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the help, unless the patient will deteriorate in that time
options.rationale: Almost nothing in a non-time-critical move is worth a spinal injury.

options.text: Attempt it and reassess if it goes badly
options.rationale: Reassessing mid-lift is exactly the failure mode.

options.text: Ask family members to help lift
options.rationale: Untrained, unequipped, and a liability problem as well as a safety one.

options.text: Drag the patient to reduce the lifting
options.rationale: Drags are emergency moves, not a workaround for being short-handed.

items.explanation_md: The question is not whether you could. It is what happens over the next twenty years if you do this twice a month.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Does this situation justify moving now with the crew you have?

rows.label: Active structure fire, patient in the room
Stable hip fracture, narrow stairs, two crew
Cardiac arrest on a soft bed in a cluttered bedroom
Heavy patient, third floor, no elevator, stable

items.explanation_md: Immediate danger and the need for a hard surface are reasons to move now. Difficulty alone is a reason to plan better, not to push through.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why is the route out often more decisive than the patient’s weight?

options.text: A narrow turn or a spiral stair can rule out the device that would otherwise have carried the weight for you
options.rationale: Space constrains the equipment, and the equipment is what makes weight manageable.

options.text: Weight does not affect the difficulty of a move
options.rationale: It clearly does.

options.text: Because routes are always the same
options.rationale: They are never the same.

options.text: Because patients rarely weigh enough to matter
options.rationale: Not true, and not the argument.

items.explanation_md: Walk the route before you commit. The second-floor landing with a ninety-degree turn is the thing that decides this call, and it is visible from the bottom of the stairs.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What should you do when you realize mid-lift that the plan is wrong?

options.text: Call a stop, set the patient down in a controlled way, and re-plan
options.rationale: A controlled abort is available at any moment and almost nobody uses it.

options.text: Push through — stopping is more dangerous
options.rationale: A controlled set-down is safer than a failing lift.

options.text: Have one person take more of the load
options.rationale: Now one person is carrying a load nobody planned for.

options.text: Speed up to shorten the exposure
options.rationale: Speed under a failing lift is how patients get dropped.

items.explanation_md: Agree the stop word before you lift. Anybody can call it, nobody argues in the moment, and it is discussed afterwards.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why estimate a patient’s weight high rather than optimistically?

options.text: An underestimate commits you to equipment and a crew size that cannot cope, and you discover it under load
options.rationale: Overestimating costs a few minutes; underestimating costs a back.

options.text: Equipment ratings are inaccurate
options.rationale: They are usually accurate — the issue is your estimate.

options.text: Patients routinely misreport their weight upward
options.rationale: Under-reporting is the more common direction.

options.text: It affects drug dosing only
options.rationale: Dosing matters and is not this block’s concern.

items.explanation_md: Every device has a rated capacity. Exceeding it is not a safety margin being tested, it is a failure being scheduled.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is the strongest argument for asking for more resources on a difficult move?

options.text: It is the one part of injury prevention with real leverage, and it costs only time
options.rationale: Technique training did not prevent injury. Not needing the lift does.

options.text: It looks thorough
options.rationale: Not a reason.

options.text: It reduces documentation
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: It is required by protocol on every call
options.rationale: It is a judgment, not a universal rule.

items.explanation_md: This is why 6.1 comes first. Once you know training does not save you, the resource decision stops being an admission and starts being the plan.
items.source_ref: Verbeek JH, Martimo K-P, Karppinen J, et al. Manual material handling advice and assistive devices for preventing and treating back pain in workers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(6):CD005958.

items.stem: What does keeping the load close to your body actually change?

options.text: The force on the spine, which rises as the weight moves further from it
options.rationale: A load at arm’s length loads the back several times more than the same load held close.

options.text: Nothing measurable
options.rationale: The effect is large and well established.

options.text: Only the effort in your arms
options.rationale: The spine is where the difference shows.

options.text: Only your balance
options.rationale: Balance improves too, and force is the point.

items.explanation_md: This is the biomechanics nobody disputes. It is worth doing on every lift; it is just not a substitute for having enough people.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select the elements of a sound lift.

options.text: Feet apart and planted, one slightly ahead
options.rationale: A stable base before anything moves.

options.text: Back in a neutral position, bending at the hips and knees
options.rationale: Load the legs rather than the lumbar spine.

options.text: Load kept close to the body throughout
options.rationale: Distance is what multiplies the force.

options.text: Lift and lower smoothly, without twisting
options.rationale: Rotation under load is a distinct injury mechanism.

options.text: Lift quickly to shorten the time under load
options.rationale: Speed removes your ability to abort.

items.explanation_md: Base, back, close, smooth. Straightforward, universally taught, and not by itself enough to keep you uninjured across a career.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Who should call the count on a team lift?

options.text: One named person, agreed before anyone takes weight, using words everyone has heard
options.rationale: One voice, agreed in advance, saying the same words every time.

options.text: Whoever is strongest
options.rationale: Strength has nothing to do with who counts.

options.text: Whoever is at the head
options.rationale: Position does not determine it either, though it is a common convention.

options.text: Nobody — people lift when ready
options.rationale: That is how one person ends up lifting alone.

items.explanation_md: Agree the words too. "Ready, set, lift" and "on three, lifting on three" give different answers to when the weight moves, and half a crew will guess wrong.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Put a coordinated team lift in order.

options.text: Agree the plan, the route and the stop word
options.rationale: Before anybody touches the patient.

options.text: Name who calls the count and confirm the words
options.rationale: One voice, agreed.

options.text: Everyone sets their base and confirms they are ready
options.rationale: A verbal yes from each person.

options.text: The count is called and the load moves together
options.rationale: Together is the whole point.

options.text: Move, then set down smoothly on a second count
options.rationale: Setting down is a lift in reverse and gets skipped.

items.explanation_md: Most dropped patients and most crew injuries happen in the setting-down phase, because everyone treats the lift as finished once it is in the air.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: You are on a four-person lift and your grip is failing. What do you say?

options.text: "Losing it — setting down on three." Name the problem and the action, immediately
options.rationale: Specific, early, and it tells three other people exactly what happens next.

options.text: Nothing, and try to hold on
options.rationale: The others cannot plan for a failure they do not know about.

options.text: "Hurry up"
options.rationale: Ambiguous, and it invites speed rather than a controlled stop.

options.text: Adjust your grip silently while holding
options.rationale: Regripping under load is when people drop things.

items.explanation_md: The same rule as chapter 4: name the specific problem, before the failure, not after. A lift is the clearest case there is.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why is twisting while carrying a load singled out as a risk?

options.text: Rotation under load stresses spinal structures in a way straight lifting does not
options.rationale: It is a separate mechanism, not just more of the same force.

options.text: It slows the move
options.rationale: Not the reason.

options.text: It only matters with heavy patients
options.rationale: It matters at modest loads too.

options.text: It is uncomfortable but harmless
options.rationale: It is one of the better established mechanisms of injury.

items.explanation_md: Move your feet. Turning the whole body takes an extra second and removes the mechanism entirely.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is the point of a stop word on a lift?

options.text: It lets anyone halt the lift without argument or explanation at the moment they need to
options.rationale: Agreed in advance so nobody has to negotiate under load.

options.text: It signals the end of the lift
options.rationale: That is the count for setting down.

options.text: It tells the patient what is happening
options.rationale: Explaining to the patient is separate and also worth doing.

options.text: It is a formality for documentation
options.rationale: It is an operational safeguard.

items.explanation_md: The value is that it removes the social cost of stopping. Nobody has to decide whether their grip failing is worth speaking up about.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why does the setting-down phase deserve as much attention as the lift?

options.text: Concentration drops once the weight is up, and a large share of drops and strains happen on the way down
options.rationale: People treat the lift as finished at the top.

options.text: Because the load is heavier going down
options.rationale: It is the same load.

options.text: Because the patient moves more
options.rationale: Not the general mechanism.

options.text: It does not — the lift is the risky part
options.rationale: That belief is the reason the setting down goes wrong.

items.explanation_md: Call a second count for setting down, every time. It costs one word and it is where the attention has already gone.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Is it better to push or to pull a loaded cot?

options.text: Push — it lets you use body weight and keeps the load in front of you where you can see it
options.rationale: Pulling loads the back and takes the load out of view.

options.text: Pull — it gives better control
options.rationale: It gives worse control and worse mechanics.

options.text: They are equivalent
options.rationale: They are not.

options.text: It depends only on the floor surface
options.rationale: Surface matters; it does not reverse the principle.

items.explanation_md: Push where you can, pull only where you must, and keep the load between waist and shoulder height while you do.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select the principles that apply when reaching for a patient.

options.text: Keep the back in a neutral position, avoiding hyperextension
options.rationale: Reaching overhead arches the back under load.

options.text: Avoid reaching more than about fifteen to twenty inches in front of the body
options.rationale: Beyond that the leverage against the spine climbs sharply.

options.text: Avoid prolonged reaching, particularly with any weight
options.rationale: Sustained reach is worse than brief.

options.text: Move yourself closer rather than extending further
options.rationale: The fix for a long reach is almost always your feet.

options.text: Twist at the waist to extend range
options.rationale: That combines the two worst mechanisms at once.

items.explanation_md: Almost every reaching problem is solved by moving your own position. Log rolls and bed-to-cot transfers are where this gets forgotten.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: You are carrying a loaded stair chair down a flight with a partner. What matters most?

options.text: Flexing at the hips rather than the waist, keeping the back locked, and moving one step at a time on a count
options.rationale: The back stays neutral and the legs do the work, on an agreed rhythm.

options.text: Moving quickly to reduce time under load
options.rationale: Speed on stairs is how both of you end up at the bottom.

options.text: Having the stronger person take the bottom
options.rationale: Convention exists; it is not what protects the backs.

options.text: Carrying with arms extended for clearance
options.rationale: That is the reaching problem, on stairs, under load.

items.explanation_md: Stairs are where the largest forces and the worst positions meet. A track stair chair, where you have one, removes most of the lift.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Sound, or a mechanism of injury?

rows.label: Moving your feet to turn rather than twisting at the waist
Reaching across a bed to log roll a patient
Pushing a cot from waist height with body weight behind it
Pulling a loaded cot up a curb from above the shoulders

items.explanation_md: The two injury mechanisms share a feature: the load is far from the body, and the spine is making up the difference.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why is a log roll a high-risk maneuver for the crew rather than only for the patient?

options.text: It combines a long reach, a sustained hold and often a twist, at bed height
options.rationale: Three mechanisms in one, repeated on most trauma calls.

options.text: Because the patient is heavy
options.rationale: Weight is a factor, and the posture is the reason this one is singled out.

options.text: Because it takes a long time
options.rationale: It is quick. That does not help.

options.text: It is not high risk for the crew
options.rationale: It is one of the most common postures associated with injury.

items.explanation_md: Get the bed to a workable height if you can, kneel on it if that is permitted, and put people on both sides. Do not solve it by reaching further.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: At what height should you push a loaded cot?

options.text: Between waist and shoulder height, where you can put body weight behind it
options.rationale: Below the waist loads the back; above the shoulders removes your leverage.

options.text: As low as possible for stability
options.rationale: Low pushing bends you forward under load.

options.text: Above shoulder height for visibility
options.rationale: It costs you the ability to push with body weight.

options.text: Height is irrelevant when pushing
options.rationale: It changes both the force and who supplies it.

items.explanation_md: The same principle as everything else in this block: get the work into the large muscles and out of the lumbar spine.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why does a sustained static hold injure people who could have lifted the same weight briefly?

options.text: Muscles fatigue under static load and the burden shifts progressively onto passive structures
options.rationale: Time under load is its own exposure.

options.text: The weight increases over time
options.rationale: It does not.

options.text: Static holds are always heavier
options.rationale: Not necessarily.

options.text: It does not — duration is irrelevant
options.rationale: Duration is a well described risk factor.

items.explanation_md: Which is why holding a door, a limb or a cot rail "just for a minute" during a long extrication is worth handing over rather than enduring.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: A cot will not roll over deep gravel to the ambulance. What is the answer?

options.text: Carry it with four people, or use a device suited to the ground, rather than forcing it with two
options.rationale: The surface has changed the task; the plan should change with it.

options.text: Push harder with two
options.rationale: This is the moment the cot tips or a back goes.

options.text: Pull it backwards over the gravel
options.rationale: Worse mechanics and the load is now behind you.

options.text: Lift one end and drag the other
options.rationale: It loads one person entirely and destabilizes the cot.

items.explanation_md: A wheeled device stops being a wheeled device on the wrong surface. Recognize that before you are halfway across it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What justifies an emergency move?

options.text: Immediate danger to the patient or crew, or the need to reach a patient whose condition requires it now
options.rationale: Fire, hazardous atmosphere, an unstable vehicle, or a patient in arrest on a surface you cannot work on.

options.text: A long carry to the ambulance
options.rationale: Difficulty is not danger.

options.text: A crew that is short-handed
options.rationale: That is a resource problem with a different answer.

options.text: A patient who is refusing to cooperate
options.rationale: Not a justification for an emergency move.

items.explanation_md: Emergency moves accept the risk of aggravating an injury because the alternative is worse. That trade only works when something really is worse.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Sort each situation by the category of move it calls for.

options.text: Fire in the structure, patient in the room
options.rationale: Immediate danger — move now, by whatever means.

options.text: Altered mental status with a compromised airway in a cramped car
options.rationale: Condition requires moving them to be treated — urgent.

options.text: Stable ankle injury, clear route to the cot
options.rationale: Non-urgent: plan it, do it properly.

options.text: Cardiac arrest on a soft bed
options.rationale: Needs a hard surface now — an emergency move for a clinical reason.

items.explanation_md: Emergency: danger now. Urgent: the condition requires moving them to treat them. Non-urgent: everything else, and most of your calls.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Which drag best protects the spine during an emergency move?

options.text: One that pulls along the long axis of the body, supporting the head and neck as far as possible
options.rationale: Clothes drag, blanket drag or shoulder drag — all pull in line with the spine.

options.text: Pulling sideways by one arm
options.rationale: It twists the spine and concentrates force on one joint.

options.text: Lifting under the arms and dragging the legs sideways
options.rationale: Sideways is the problem.

options.text: Dragging by the ankles
options.rationale: The head is unsupported and the spine is loaded in the wrong direction.

items.explanation_md: You are accepting risk to the spine, not ignoring it. Pull along the long axis and take the head with you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select the situations where a rapid extrication from a vehicle is appropriate.

options.text: The scene is unsafe — fire, fuel, an unstable vehicle
options.rationale: Danger outweighs the risk of the move.

options.text: The patient’s condition needs care that cannot be given in the vehicle
options.rationale: Airway or arrest in a seated patient.

options.text: The patient blocks access to a more critically injured patient
options.rationale: A recognized indication.

options.text: The patient is deteriorating and transport cannot wait for a controlled extrication
options.rationale: Time-critical condition.

options.text: The patient wants to get out of the car
options.rationale: Understandable, and not an indication for rapid extrication.

items.explanation_md: Four indications, all of them about danger or time. Rapid extrication is not the default for a patient who happens to be in a car.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: A patient in cardiac arrest is on a soft bed. What do you do first?

options.text: Move them to the floor, or get a hard surface under the chest, before compressions
options.rationale: Compressions on a soft mattress dissipate into the mattress.

options.text: Start compressions on the bed and move when help arrives
options.rationale: You will be delivering ineffective compressions for minutes.

options.text: Raise the bed to working height and compress there
options.rationale: Height does not fix compliance of the surface.

options.text: Wait for a backboard
options.rationale: The floor is available now.

items.explanation_md: This is the clearest clinical reason for an emergency move that has nothing to do with danger. The surface is the problem.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is the cost of choosing an emergency move when it was not needed?

options.text: You accept a real risk of worsening an injury, for no benefit that could not have been had by planning
options.rationale: The trade only pays when the alternative is genuinely worse.

options.text: There is no cost — faster is always safer
options.rationale: That reasoning is how patients get hurt during moves.

options.text: Only a documentation problem
options.rationale: The harm is physical.

options.text: Only a cost to the crew
options.rationale: Both patient and crew.

items.explanation_md: Every emergency move is a decision to trade one risk for another. Naming which risk you are buying down keeps that decision honest.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What defines an urgent move, as distinct from an emergency one?

options.text: The patient’s condition requires moving them in order to assess or treat, without immediate external danger
options.rationale: Condition-driven rather than scene-driven.

options.text: The crew is in a hurry
options.rationale: Not a category of move.

options.text: It is any move done within five minutes
options.rationale: Time is not the definition.

options.text: It requires a backboard
options.rationale: Equipment does not define the category.

items.explanation_md: The three categories sort by *why* you are moving: danger, condition, or neither. The equipment follows from that, not the other way round.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What should the record show about an emergency move?

options.text: What the danger or clinical necessity was, and what move was used
options.rationale: The justification is the part that matters afterward.

options.text: Only that the patient was moved
options.rationale: It leaves the decision unexplained.

options.text: Nothing — moves are routine
options.rationale: An emergency move is not routine.

options.text: Only the time of the move
options.rationale: Time without reason explains nothing.

items.explanation_md: Chapter 4 again: write the reasoning, not only the action. "Rapid extrication due to fuel leak and deteriorating airway" is a defensible sentence.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Match each situation to the most appropriate device.

options.text: Conscious patient, no spinal concern, narrow staircase
options.rationale: A stair chair fits where a cot cannot.

options.text: Suspected pelvic or femoral injury, needs lifting with minimal movement
options.rationale: A scoop splits and closes under the patient.

options.text: Unstable spinal injury, long transport, needs conforming support
options.rationale: A vacuum mattress conforms and distributes pressure.

options.text: Stable patient, level route to the ambulance
options.rationale: The cot, which is what it is for.

items.explanation_md: The space, the injury and the distance pick the device between them. Most poor choices come from picking the device first.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is the advantage of a scoop stretcher over a log roll onto a board?

options.text: It can be assembled under the patient with far less movement of the spine
options.rationale: It splits, slides under from both sides, and closes.

options.text: It is more comfortable for long transport
options.rationale: A vacuum mattress is better for that.

options.text: It is lighter than a backboard
options.rationale: Weight is not the clinical advantage.

options.text: It provides better immobilization
options.rationale: That is not its distinguishing feature either.

items.explanation_md: Less movement to get the patient onto it is the whole case for it, and it is a good one — particularly with a suspected pelvic injury.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Which position fits the patient?

rows.label: Conscious patient in respiratory distress
Unresponsive patient breathing adequately, no spinal concern
Hypotensive patient with no respiratory distress
Patient vomiting, unable to protect their airway

items.explanation_md: Position is treatment. Laying a breathless patient flat because the cot is flat is one of the more common avoidable harms in this chapter.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: A conscious patient in severe respiratory distress refuses to lie flat for transport. What do you do?

options.text: Transport them sitting up — their position is a treatment they are administering to themselves
options.rationale: Forcing a breathless patient flat can be actively harmful.

options.text: Insist on supine for safety during transport
options.rationale: Restraint straps do not require a supine patient.

options.text: Document a refusal of care
options.rationale: They are not refusing care; they are refusing a position.

options.text: Lay them flat once they are secured
options.rationale: Same harm, delayed.

items.explanation_md: Patients in distress adopt the position that works. Overriding it for tidiness is the error, and it is a common one.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select what must be true before you move a loaded wheeled cot.

options.text: The patient is secured with all straps, including across the chest and legs
options.rationale: All of them, every time.

options.text: Rails are up and equipment is secured
options.rationale: Loose equipment on a cot becomes a projectile.

options.text: The cot is at a height you can control, and both crew are in position
options.rationale: Height and hands before movement.

options.text: The route has been checked for the obstacle you have not seen yet
options.rationale: Thresholds, curbs, gravel, ice.

options.text: The patient has consented to each strap individually
options.rationale: Explain what you are doing; this is not a consent procedure per strap.

items.explanation_md: Cot tip-overs with a patient aboard are a recurring and entirely preventable event. Straps, rails, height, route.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why position a patient with suspected shock supine rather than with the legs elevated?

options.text: Leg elevation has not been shown to produce a clinically meaningful benefit, and supine with warmth and rapid transport is what is supported
options.rationale: The historical shock position has not held up.

options.text: Leg elevation causes airway compromise
options.rationale: Not the reason it fell out of favor.

options.text: It is impossible on a cot
options.rationale: It is quite possible.

options.text: Because the patient will be uncomfortable
options.rationale: Comfort is not the issue.

items.explanation_md: Another practice that survived on plausibility. Keep them flat, keep them warm, and get moving — the transport is the intervention.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why does a vacuum mattress suit a long transport better than a rigid board?

options.text: It conforms to the patient and spreads pressure, where a rigid board concentrates it and causes pain and tissue injury
options.rationale: Board-related pain and pressure injury are well described.

options.text: It restricts motion more completely
options.rationale: That is not its advantage.

options.text: It is faster to apply
options.rationale: It is usually slower.

options.text: It is radiolucent and boards are not
options.rationale: Not the distinguishing point here.

items.explanation_md: Rigid boards cause measurable harm over time — pain, pressure areas, respiratory restriction. That is why 6.7 spends most of its length on getting people off them.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: What is the practical limit that decides whether a stair chair or a cot goes up?

options.text: The geometry of the route — width, turns and landings — not the patient’s weight
options.rationale: A cot that cannot turn the landing is not an option at any weight.

options.text: The patient’s weight alone
options.rationale: Weight matters and geometry is what rules a device out.

options.text: The number of crew
options.rationale: Crew affects whether you can, not whether it fits.

options.text: The patient’s preference
options.rationale: Worth hearing, not decisive.

items.explanation_md: Walk it first. The device decision is made at the bottom of the stairs, which is also where you can still change it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is the goal of spinal motion restriction, as currently described?

options.text: Keeping the head, neck and torso in alignment — which several devices can achieve
options.rationale: Alignment is the objective; the long board is one means among several.

options.text: Complete elimination of all spinal movement
options.rationale: Not achievable, and not the stated goal.

options.text: Securing every patient with a mechanism of injury to a long board
options.rationale: That is the practice current guidance moved away from.

options.text: Preventing the patient from moving at all during transport
options.rationale: Overstates it and describes restraint rather than alignment.

items.explanation_md: The change of language is the change of practice. Restriction of motion, achieved by any adequate means, replaced immobilization on a specific device.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: A patient has a penetrating injury to the neck and no neurological deficit. What does current guidance say about spinal motion restriction?

options.text: There is no role for it in penetrating trauma — it delays transport and has been associated with worse outcomes
options.rationale: Stated plainly in the joint position statement.

options.text: Apply a collar and board as for blunt trauma
options.rationale: This is the specific practice the guidance rejects.

options.text: Apply a collar only
options.rationale: Still not indicated, and it obscures the neck you need to watch.

options.text: Decide based on the weapon used
options.rationale: Not the basis for the recommendation.

items.explanation_md: This is the single most consequential line in the block. Penetrating trauma patients need to be somewhere else quickly, and the collar buys nothing.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: Select the findings that support restricting spinal motion after blunt trauma.

options.text: Midline spinal pain or tenderness
options.rationale: A core indication.

options.text: Any neurological complaint or finding — numbness, weakness, tingling
options.rationale: The finding you cannot afford to miss.

options.text: Altered mental status, including intoxication
options.rationale: You cannot clear a spine you cannot examine.

options.text: A distracting injury, or anatomic deformity of the spine
options.rationale: Both limit the reliability of your assessment.

options.text: Any motor vehicle collision, regardless of findings
options.rationale: Mechanism alone stopped being an indication.

items.explanation_md: Findings, not mechanism. That shift is what separates current practice from the version that boarded everybody who had been in a car.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: What is the argument against routine use of the long backboard for transport?

options.text: It causes measurable harm — pain, pressure injury, respiratory restriction — without demonstrated benefit for most patients
options.rationale: Harm is documented; benefit for routine use is not.

options.text: It is too expensive
options.rationale: Cost is not the argument.

options.text: It takes too long to apply
options.rationale: Time matters and is not the main case.

options.text: It is uncomfortable, which is a minor consideration
options.rationale: The harms are more than discomfort.

items.explanation_md: The board remains useful as an extrication tool. The change is that being extricated on one is not a reason to be transported on one.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: Does this patient need spinal motion restriction?

rows.label: Gunshot wound to the abdomen, alert, no deficit
Fall from a ladder, midline thoracic tenderness
Low-speed collision, no pain, no deficit, fully alert
Collision, intoxicated, cannot give a reliable examination

items.explanation_md: Two of these turn on findings. One turns on the fact that the assessment cannot be trusted. And one is penetrating trauma, where the answer is no regardless.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: Which devices can achieve adequate spinal motion restriction?

options.text: A vacuum mattress, a scoop stretcher, or the ambulance cot with the patient secured and aligned
options.rationale: Alignment is the goal, and several devices reach it.

options.text: Only a long backboard with head blocks
options.rationale: That is the practice the guidance moved away from.

options.text: A cervical collar alone in every case
options.rationale: A collar alone does not restrict torso motion.

options.text: Only a vacuum mattress
options.rationale: It is one good option, not the only one.

items.explanation_md: Naming the goal rather than the device is what allows a crew to use what fits the patient and the space in front of them.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: How should you describe the evidence base for spinal motion restriction itself?

options.text: Long-established practice with potential for significant harm and without definitive evidence of clinical benefit
options.rationale: That is how a recent literature review characterizes it, and saying so is honest.

options.text: Strongly supported by randomized trials
options.rationale: No such trial base exists.

options.text: Proven to prevent secondary spinal injury
options.rationale: Not demonstrated.

options.text: Disproven and abandoned everywhere
options.rationale: It remains indicated in defined circumstances.

items.explanation_md: Both things are true at once: it is indicated by current guidance in defined situations, and the evidence that it helps is thin. Being able to hold both is the skill.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: A patient was extricated on a long board and now has no indications for spinal motion restriction. What next?

options.text: Take them off it for transport, in line with protocol — extrication and transport are separate decisions
options.rationale: The board did a job; that job is finished.

options.text: Leave them on it, since removing risks movement
options.rationale: The transport harms accumulate and the indication is absent.

options.text: Leave them on it to save time
options.rationale: Not a clinical reason.

options.text: Leave them on it because the hospital expects it
options.rationale: Expectation is not an indication.

items.explanation_md: Extrication tool, not a transport surface. That one sentence carries most of the practical change in this block.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: A patient meeting indications is agitated and fighting the collar and straps. What is the concern?

options.text: Fighting restraint can produce more spinal movement than leaving them in a position of comfort under observation
options.rationale: Restriction that provokes struggling can defeat its own purpose.

options.text: The straps will fail
options.rationale: Not the primary concern.

options.text: It delays transport only
options.rationale: The delay matters less than the movement.

options.text: There is no concern — restriction must be maintained
options.rationale: Not if maintaining it causes what it was meant to prevent.

items.explanation_md: Consider why they are agitated — hypoxia and head injury are on that list — and weigh whether forcing the device is achieving anything.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: What is the first thing to establish before moving a bariatric patient?

options.text: Whether your equipment is rated for the weight, and how many people and what device the move needs
options.rationale: Rated capacity is a limit, not a suggestion.

options.text: Whether the patient can walk
options.rationale: Relevant, and it does not come before the equipment question.

options.text: Which hospital will accept them
options.rationale: Destination matters and is not the first handling question.

options.text: How long the move will take
options.rationale: Not the deciding factor.

items.explanation_md: Most services have a bariatric resource and a rated capacity for every device. Knowing both before the call is what makes the decision quick.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Select what a bariatric move needs beyond a standard one.

options.text: Equipment rated for the actual weight, not close to it
options.rationale: Exceeding a rating is a scheduled failure.

options.text: More hands, requested early rather than once you are committed
options.rationale: Early, because the wait is the cost.

options.text: A route assessed for width, floor strength and turns
options.rationale: Including whether the floor and stairs will take it.

options.text: Care that the patient is not talked about as a problem in front of them
options.rationale: They can hear you, and they have heard it before.

options.text: A faster move to limit time under load
options.rationale: Speed is exactly what should not increase.

items.explanation_md: The fourth is not decoration. Bariatric patients routinely report being discussed as an object during a move, and it changes whether they call next time.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What is different about securing an infant or small child for transport?

options.text: Adult cot straps do not fit them — a size-appropriate restraint device is needed
options.rationale: An unsecured child in the compartment is a projectile.

options.text: They can be held by a parent during transport
options.rationale: Being held is not restraint, and in a crash the child is lost.

options.text: Adult straps work if tightened fully
options.rationale: They do not restrain a small body.

options.text: Children do not need restraint on short transports
options.rationale: Crash forces do not care about distance.

items.explanation_md: A parent holding a child in a moving ambulance cannot hold them in a collision. This is one of the clearest examples of a comfortable practice that fails at the moment it matters.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Which handling consideration applies?

rows.label: Check the rated capacity of every device in the chain
Use a size-appropriate restraint rather than adult straps
Handle limbs gently — fragile skin and osteoporotic bone
Pad to accommodate kyphosis rather than forcing the patient flat

items.explanation_md: Two of these are about the equipment fitting the patient. Two are about the patient’s tissue not tolerating what the equipment assumes.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: An older patient with a marked kyphosis cannot lie flat on the cot. What do you do?

options.text: Pad under the head and shoulders to support the position they actually have
options.rationale: Forcing them flat risks fracture and is painful and unnecessary.

options.text: Strap them down flat for transport safety
options.rationale: That is how you fracture a spine during a move.

options.text: Transport them sitting in a stair chair instead
options.rationale: Sometimes appropriate; it is not the general answer.

options.text: Ask them to straighten as much as they can
options.rationale: The curvature is fixed, and asking is asking the impossible.

items.explanation_md: Pad to the patient. A cot is a flat surface, and the patient is not obliged to become one.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Why is skin integrity a handling consideration in older patients?

options.text: Thin, fragile skin tears and bruises from grip and shear that would not mark a younger patient
options.rationale: Sliding transfers and tight grips are the usual causes.

options.text: It affects drug absorption
options.rationale: Not a handling matter.

options.text: It only matters with diabetes
options.rationale: It is a general feature of aging skin.

options.text: It does not affect how you move them
options.rationale: It changes grip, surfaces and transfer technique.

items.explanation_md: Use a slide sheet or a scoop rather than dragging on skin, and grip broad areas rather than pinching limbs. A skin tear on an older patient is a real injury.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: What do bariatric, pediatric and geriatric handling have in common?

options.text: The standard equipment and the standard plan assume a patient none of them is
options.rationale: Each one needs the plan changed before the move, not during it.

options.text: All three require more crew members
options.rationale: Bariatric usually does; the others often do not.

options.text: All three are emergency moves
options.rationale: They are not.

options.text: All three require a backboard
options.rationale: None of them does, as such.

items.explanation_md: Which brings this chapter back to 6.2. The resource and equipment decision is where every one of these is handled, and it is made before anyone lifts.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: A parent asks to hold their two-year-old on the cot during transport. What do you say?

options.text: No, and explain why — in a crash they cannot hold on, and the child becomes unrestrained
options.rationale: Explain it rather than just refusing; parents accept the reason.

options.text: Yes, if the parent is belted
options.rationale: The parent being belted does not restrain the child.

options.text: Yes, for short transports only
options.rationale: Distance does not change crash forces.

options.text: Yes, if the child is distressed otherwise
options.rationale: Distress is real and it is not a reason to leave a child unrestrained.

items.explanation_md: Seat the parent where the child can see and touch them. That solves most of the distress without solving it by removing the restraint.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

stimulus.text:
0210. A single-vehicle collision into a ditch off a rural road. The car is upright and stable, no fuel leak, no fire.

The driver is a 58-year-old man, alert, oriented, complaining of pain across his lower back. He has no numbness or weakness anywhere, and no other injuries you can find. He weighs, by his own account, about 280 pounds, and he is sitting in a car with the driver door jammed shut.

The ditch is soft and about four feet deep. Your cot is on the road above it. There are two of you and the nearest additional unit is fourteen minutes out. The patient is asking you to help him climb out.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Does this call justify a rapid extrication?

options.text: No — the scene is stable, he is alert with no deficit, and nothing about his condition demands it now
options.rationale: The indications are danger, condition, access or deterioration. None applies.

options.text: Yes, because the door is jammed
options.rationale: A jammed door is a logistics problem, not an emergency.

options.text: Yes, because the ditch is soft
options.rationale: Difficulty is not danger.

options.text: Yes, because you are short-handed
options.rationale: That is an argument for waiting, not for hurrying.

items.explanation_md: Everything here is difficult and nothing is dangerous. That distinction is the whole of 6.5.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Does he meet indications for spinal motion restriction?

options.text: Yes — midline lower back pain after blunt trauma is an indication, even with no deficit
options.rationale: Findings, not mechanism, and he has a finding.

options.text: No, because he has no neurological deficit
options.rationale: Deficit is one indication among several, not a requirement.

options.text: No, because he is alert and oriented
options.rationale: Alertness makes the examination reliable; it does not negate the finding.

options.text: Yes, but only because of the mechanism
options.rationale: Mechanism alone is no longer an indication. The pain is.

items.explanation_md: Midline spinal pain is a core indication. What follows is a question about alignment and device, not about whether to do it at all.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: He asks you to help him climb out of the car. What do you say?

options.text: No, and explain why — self-extrication would produce exactly the motion you are trying to restrict
options.rationale: Explain it; patients generally accept a reason.

options.text: Yes, it saves the lift and the movement is minimal
options.rationale: Climbing out of a car seat is not minimal spinal movement.

options.text: Yes, if he moves slowly
options.rationale: Slowly is still the movement you are trying to avoid.

options.text: Yes, if he holds his own neck
options.rationale: It does not restrict the thoracolumbar motion that his pain points at.

items.explanation_md: There is a real debate about self-extrication in patients with no findings. This patient has a finding, which puts him outside it.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: What has to be answered before anybody takes weight here?

options.text: His actual weight, estimated high rather than optimistically
options.rationale: 280 by his own account means plan for more.

options.text: The route — out of a four-foot soft ditch, up to a road
options.rationale: This is the constraint that decides everything else.

options.text: Whether two people is enough, and what fourteen minutes costs
options.rationale: He is stable, so the wait is affordable.

options.text: Which device works: a scoop assembled under him, or a vacuum mattress
options.rationale: Both achieve alignment with less movement than a log roll.

options.text: How quickly the call can be cleared
options.rationale: Not a factor in how he gets moved.

items.explanation_md: Weight, route, hands, device. On this call the route and the weight together answer the hands question for you.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Two of you, 280 pounds, a soft four-foot ditch, and help fourteen minutes away. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for the second unit — he is stable, and nothing about fourteen minutes harms him
options.rationale: This is the resource decision, and it is the one with real leverage.

options.text: Attempt it with two and reassess if it goes badly
options.rationale: Reassessing mid-lift out of a ditch is the failure mode.

options.text: Ask bystanders to help carry him up the bank
options.rationale: Untrained hands on an uneven slope with a spinal indication.

options.text: Have him self-extricate to avoid the lift entirely
options.rationale: Already ruled out by his findings.

items.explanation_md: Fourteen minutes costs this patient nothing. The alternative costs two crews a lift they will remember in twenty years.
items.source_ref: Verbeek JH, Martimo K-P, Karppinen J, et al. Manual material handling advice and assistive devices for preventing and treating back pain in workers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(6):CD005958.

items.stem: Which device best fits this patient and this extraction?

options.text: A scoop stretcher assembled under him, or a vacuum mattress — either achieves alignment with minimal movement
options.rationale: And both are practical to carry up a bank with four people.

options.text: A long backboard, because he needs immobilization
options.rationale: Alignment is the goal and the board is not required to reach it.

options.text: A stair chair, since he is seated
options.rationale: It is not a spinal device and he has a spinal indication.

options.text: Walk him to the cot supported by two crew
options.rationale: The movement you are avoiding is exactly the movement that would produce.

items.explanation_md: If a board is used to get him out of the ditch, it is an extrication tool. He does not stay on it for transport.
items.source_ref: Fischer PE, Perina DG, Delbridge TR, et al. Spinal motion restriction in the trauma patient — a joint position statement (ACS-COT, ACEP, NAEMSP). Prehosp Emerg Care 2018;22(6):659–61.

items.stem: Four people are now carrying him up a soft bank. What keeps that lift together?

options.text: One named person calling an agreed count, an agreed stop word, and a second count for setting down
options.rationale: One voice, agreed words, and an abort available at any moment.

options.text: Everyone lifting when they feel ready
options.rationale: That is how one person carries the load alone.

options.text: Moving as fast as possible up the bank
options.rationale: Speed removes the ability to stop.

options.text: The strongest person taking the heavy end and setting the pace
options.rationale: Strength does not decide who counts.

items.explanation_md: Uneven ground is precisely where someone loses footing. The stop word exists so the person who does can say so without deciding whether it is worth mentioning.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Lifting and Moving Patients.

items.stem: Reviewing this call, which decision did the most to prevent injury?

options.text: Waiting for the second unit — the resource decision, made before anyone took weight
options.rationale: Technique training does not prevent injury. Not lifting it with two people does.

options.text: Lifting with the legs rather than the back
options.rationale: Sound for one lift, and not what the evidence says prevents career injury.

options.text: Choosing a scoop over a backboard
options.rationale: The right call clinically, and it is about the patient rather than the crew.

options.text: Calling a clear count
options.rationale: It keeps the lift together; it does not reduce the load.

items.explanation_md: Everything else in this chapter is about doing a lift well. This is about arranging not to do it at all, and it is the only part with good evidence behind it.
items.source_ref: Verbeek JH, Martimo K-P, Karppinen J, et al. Manual material handling advice and assistive devices for preventing and treating back pain in workers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(6):CD005958.
